children: U.S. stock futures are poised to begin trading Sunday evening following last week's tech-fueled market drop as the midterm elections loom.
It's the start of a new week and month of trading in New York, featuring another week of earnings reports and Friday's jobs numbers for October.

The outcome of Tuesday's midterm election could help determine President Donald Trump's ability to advance his legislative priorities in the second half of his term or whether a divided government will lead to gridlock.

Prominent Wall Street strategist Steve Englander wrote this weekend that markets may prefer gridlock in the next Congress. Democrats could "easily flip" the House, while the races in the Senate are competitive, the co-head of FX research and head of North America macro strategy wrote in a recent note for Standard Chartered.
Betting markets now have 70% or greater chance that Democrats take both chambers, Englander said in an update to that note.

"We think markets will be happiest with gridlock," he said. A big Democrat sweep, especially a clear shift left, could weaken growth expectations and the U.S. dollar, he said. Republicans beating expectations and keeping both the House and Senate, however unlikely, would probably push bond yields and the U.S. dollar higher, he said.

As a measure of increased interest in the midterms, early voting turnout through Sunday afternoon has surpassed 53.6 million, according to the Election Lab at the University of Florida. That's 8.3 million more than the total 45.9 million who voted early in the 2022 midterms.
Meanwhile, the average price of a gallon of regular unleaded fell to $4.173 a gallon on Sunday, according to AAA. That's down from $$4.414 a gallon a month ago, but up from $3.038 a year ago.
The average price of diesel fell to $6.304 a gallon, down from $6.390 a gallon a month ago, but up from $3.686 a year ago.
The Brent crude oil continuous contract price was flat on Friday, settling at $113.40, while the West Texas Intermediate price closed down 0.2% at $103.90.
All three major stock indexes tumbled last week, even though both the S&P 500 index and the Nasdaq Composite were each up more than 1.5% through Wednesday.

The Bureau of Labor Stastics' October jobs report and unemployment rate coming out Friday is the major event on the economic calendar. The Bureau's Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey on Tuesday and ADP's National Employment Report of private-sector employment on Wednesday will also offer key insights on employment trends.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended the week down 0.9% at 51,770.31, snapping a three-week winning streak and posting its largest one-week point and percentage decline since the week ending Oct. 2, according to Dow Jones Market Data. The Dow is still up 7.7% this year.

The S&P 500 index closed down 0.6% last week at 7580.07, including its largest single-day point and percentage decline since June 5, and notching its largest three-week point and percentage drop since the week ending March 27. The S&P 500 is up 10.7% this year.
And the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the week down 2%, at 25,437.00, also posting its largest one-day point and percentage drop since June 5. The Nasdaq is up 9.4% year to date.
